summary: The Italian military said Friday that its navy had recovered the fishing boat Airone hours after armed men seized it off Sicily. The boat was intercepted about 90 kilometers (56 miles) from Libya's port of Misrata, and a naval unit detained a Libyan soldier aboard, Italian military statements said. The navy said accidental rifle fire during the operation slightly injured one of the seven fishermen. The crew comprised three Sicilians and four Tunisians who had left Mazara del Vallo five days earlier to fish for shrimp.

(CNN)Novak Djokovic extended his current winning streak to 17 matches after beating Thomas Berdych 7-5, 4-6, 6-3 in the rain-interrupted final of the Monte Carlo Masters. "It was a tough match, a particular match," said Djokovic after winning his 52nd career title, and his second Monte Carlo Masters championship. After winning the Australian Open back in January, Djokovic has followed up with Masters' victories at Indian Wells and Miami. Sunday's victory over Berdych means he becomes the first man to win the opening three Masters tournaments of the season.

Former Satyam Computers Services chairman Ramalinga Raju and nine others received seven-year prison sentences, and Raju was fined $804,000, Indian officials said. The case involved a $1.6 billion fraud exposed in 2009 when Raju admitted overstating profits through invented assets and cash, although investigators say investors' losses were much greater. The Central Bureau of Investigation said a special court convicted the defendants of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other offenses. After Raju's disclosures, the government dismissed Satyam's board, and Tech Mahindra acquired what had been India's fourth-largest software services provider through a state-backed auction.

Photographer Johan Bavman used his photography to document the real-life experience of fathers taking full advantage of Sweden's parental leave program, which grants a total of 480 calendar days, with 390 of them paid at 80% of income and 60 mandated as "daddy months" or "partner months." In reality, only 12% of Swedish couples equally share the 480 days of leave, Bavman said; he is looking for a total of 60 fathers to photograph for an exhibition and a book, has found 35 so far, and wants realistic imagery showing their devotion and tiredness.

Officials said ISIS freed more than 200 Yazidis in northern Iraq on Wednesday, mostly women and children alongside sick or elderly captives, with Kurdistan Regional Government official Nuri Osman reporting 217 releases and Peshmerga commander Rassol Omar reporting 228. The reason was unclear, though Omar said Arab tribal leaders helped arrange the release, and Peshmerga forces received the freed captives and sent them to Irbil, Osman said.

Philadelphia police added attempted murder to the charges against Nyia Parler, 41, alleging she left her 21-year-old son, who has quadriplegia and cerebral palsy, in Cobbs Creek Park for more than four days while visiting her boyfriend in Maryland. Her son was found Friday suffering from dehydration, malnutrition and other injuries, police said, while Maryland authorities said Parler, taken into custody Sunday, must finish unspecified treatment before extradition to Philadelphia.

New research released by the Anne Frank House concluded that Anne and her older sister, Margot Frank, probably did not survive to March 1945, contradicting the previously determined March 31, 1945, date of Anne's death. Witnesses at the camp said the sisters both had symptoms of typhus before February 7, but the exact dates of death for Anne and Margot remain unclear.

Bundchen walked the runway for the last time Wednesday, and the New England Patriots quarterback wasn't just there to support her in person, he expressed his emotions to the world on Facebook. Bundchen, 34, announced her retirement from the catwalk last weekend.

French police said Saturday that investigators had finished collecting the principal evidence from the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site and were not expected to return. The March 24 crash in the Alps near Seyne-les-Alpes killed all 150 people aboard, and a private security company will guard the site until the remaining wreckage is removed. The flight data recorder was recovered Thursday, following the earlier discovery of the cockpit voice recorder. Prosecutor Brice Robin said laboratories had identified 150 DNA profiles from more than 2,000 samples and that investigators had recovered 470 personal belongings, including 40 badly damaged cell phones. Robin doubted the phones would yield useful information. Authorities say co-pilot Andreas Lubitz locked the captain out and deliberately crashed the aircraft. According to the BEA, initial analysis of the flight data recorder showed Lubitz intentionally accelerated the descent using the controls. Lubitz had experienced depression years earlier and had withheld recent medical notes declaring him unfit for work from his employer.

With his early leap into the 2016 race, Marco Rubio is positioning himself as the next generation of GOP leadership. Yet Rubio has been his own worst enemy on what could have been his two signature issues: immigration reform and Cuba relations. Back in 2013, Rubio was a member of the Senate "Gang of 8" that crafted a bipartisan proposal for comprehensive reform, including a path to citizenship for the nation's estimated 11 million undocumented immigrants. He later distanced himself from the bill after it ran into resistance from House Republicans, and now says he favors a piecemeal approach, starting with securing the border. No wonder the research firm Latino Decisions reports that, "We find no evidence that Rubio's candidacy will draw significant Latino support for his candidacy or for his party more generally." He has warned that Cuba is taking advantage of the United States. Most Americans support better relations with Cuba, as do a majority of Cuban-Americans. Another Rubio weakness is his lack of bold policy proposals. Unfortunately, a fresh face on stale ideas is not a winning combination -- not for Rubio, and not for Latino voters.

Ol Pejeta Conservancy, Kenya (CNN)At first glance, Sudan looks like any other northern white rhino: stout and agile, with square lips. He's the last known male northern white rhino left in the entire world. Sudan's female companions,  Fatu and Najin, live at the conservancy, where experts are scrambling to ensure the subspecies does not go extinct. A committee at the conservancy is also looking at various alternative reproduction techniques, including in vitro fertilization.

President Obama and his Cuban counterpart, Raul Castro, greeted each other and shook hands Friday night at a dinner for Latin American leaders convening in Panama City for the Summit of the Americas. During their phone call Wednesday, Obama and Castro discussed the ongoing process of normalizing relations between the United States and Cuba, according to Deputy National Security Adviser Ben Rhodes. They are expected to spend a lot more time together on Saturday, with their interactions representing the highest-level talks between the United States and Cuba since a meeting between then-Vice President Richard Nixon and then-Prime Minister Fidel Castro in 1959. Obama is expected to announce he is removing Cuba from the United States' list of countries that sponsor terrorism, but said Thursday a panel of experts was reviewing the State Department report before he makes a final determination.

Jamal al-Labani had hoped to bring his pregnant wife and 2-year-daughter back to the United States from war-torn Yemen, but family members identified him as a victim killed in a mortar strike last week in Aden. Early Tuesday evening, the 45-year-old al-Labani was on his way back from mosque prayers when he was hit in the back by shrapnel from a mortar shell, his family said, and he died minutes later. For the past three weeks, al-Labani had told family members he was concerned about not being able to evacuate as the situation deteriorated, according to his cousin Mohammed Alazzani. More than 200 people have been killed in Aden in the past 11 days, according to Naef Al Bakri, Aden's deputy governor. The Council on American-Islamic Relations said Yemeni-Americans trapped in the conflict haven't gotten enough help from the U.S. government. Responding to the criticism, the U.S. State Department said there are no current plans to evacuate private U.S. citizens from Yemen and encouraged citizens to shelter in a secure location until they can depart safely. Violence is intensifying as Saudi Arabia and other Arab nations target Houthi rebels with airstrikes, and some 16 million Yemenis living in provinces under Houthi control remained without power after an electrical blackout that began Saturday night. The International Committee of the Red Cross said Sunday that Saudi Arabia has signed off on the delivery of medical supplies and personnel to Yemen.

Law enforcement officials said Saturday that the FBI was examining a possible terrorist threat in the United States inspired by ISIS. Intercepted communications and other intelligence prompted the inquiry, but no arrests had been made, the threat's precise nature was unknown, and officials could not establish whether it was an actual plan or an aspiration. One official said the concern centered on parts of California, where security had been increased. The Transportation Security Administration notified local agencies responsible for security outside airports, although officials cautioned that the possible threat was not necessarily connected to aviation. Some other cities also strengthened security as a precaution. A Department of Homeland Security spokesman declined to discuss specifics but described measures taken in recent months, including extra screening at selected overseas airports, more random searches on U.S.-bound flights and additional safeguards in the Electronic System for Travel Authorization. He also cited a more visible law enforcement presence at federal facilities since February and outreach to local authorities and community leaders to counter violent extremism.

Lewis Hamilton took victory for Mercedes at the Chinese Grand Prix, capturing his 35th grand prix win with a pole-to-flag win under Shanghai's sunny skies. Nico Rosberg came home second, while Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel finished third to collect his third straight podium of 2015. Vettel is just 13 points behind Hamilton in the world championship and four points ahead of Rosberg, after the first three races of the year. Rosberg complained after the race that Hamilton's slow driving was holding him up, pushing him back toward Vettel and taking life out of his tyres. Hamilton said he did not do anything intentionally to slow the cars down and that Rosberg could have tried to get by, but did not. Hamilton has won two grands prix in 2015 while Rosberg has yet to climb onto the top step of the podium. Rosberg has the chance to exorcise his frustrations at the Bahrain Grand Prix in seven days, where Ferrari will hope hot track temperatures help them topple Mercedes again. Further down the field, Fernando Alonso finished his first race for the McLaren Honda partnership with 12th place in China, after missing the Australian Grand Prix because of a head injury sustained in testing and retiring in Malaysia.

(CNN)Universal's "Furious 7" continues to build momentum at the Friday box office for a weekend debut in the $135 million-$138 million range, the largest opening in North America since fall 2013. The final film featuring the late Paul Walker, "Furious 7" is opening around the globe this weekend and earned a record-breaking $60 million internationally on Wednesday and Thursday for a possible worldwide debut approaching or crossing $300 million by the end of Easter Sunday.

Steve Esmond is in stable condition and improving as his two teenage boys remain in critical condition after they became sick, perhaps from pesticide exposure, during a trip to St. John in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The teens' mother, Theresa Devine, was treated at a hospital and released, and is in occupational therapy, the family's attorney James Maron said. EPA spokesman Elias Rodriguez said preliminary test results showed the presence of methyl bromide in the family's rented villa at the Sirenusa resort; the pesticide is not allowed to be used indoors. The EPA is investigating whether the family was made ill after a fumigation at the resort on March 18 and whether environmental regulations or laws were violated, and the U.S. Department of Justice has initiated a criminal investigation.

In an audio message released Sunday, al Qaeda confirmed that two of its leaders, known as Ustad Ahmad Farooq and Qari Abdullah Mansur, were killed in CIA drone strikes in January in North Waziristan, near the Afghan-Pakistan border. Al Qaeda's South Asia branch is relatively new, announced with some fanfare back in September by al Qaeda's top leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri. The deaths of the two men continue the decimation of al Qaeda's bench of leaders. On Monday, in the southern Pakistani city of Karachi, local al Qaeda commander Nurul Hassan was killed in a raid, said Arif Hanif, district inspector general of police. Florida-raised Adnan Shukrijumah, 39, who was in charge of al Qaeda's operations to attack the West, was killed in December in a Pakistani military operation. To be sure, al Qaeda's Yemen-based affiliate, al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, or AQAP, continues to pose a threat to American aviation. The group also trained one of the gunmen who attacked the offices of the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo in Paris in January, killing 12, but it's not clear if AQAP had any direct role in planning this attack. Meanwhile, ISIS continues to attract Western recruits and also inspire "homegrown" terrorists in the West, but the core al Qaeda organization that killed almost 3,000 men, women and children on 9/11 is on life support.
